source.title: Layer-Wise Conditioning Analysis in Exploring the Learning Dynamics of DNNs
source.authors: Lei Huang; Jie Qin; Li Liu; Fan Zhu; Ling Shao

record.file_problem: Full text is present, including appendices; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares training dynamics and training loss across normalization, initialization, and residual-network settings, using layer-wise curvature measurements rather than the claim versions’ main classification-error measures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports layer-wise conditioning results and training-loss curves. The weight-domination experiments block updates deliberately; those results do not establish how the unmodified networks train and are not included as claim-version rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own initialization, normalization and residual-depth training experiments. Training-loss comparisons address optimization behavior, and additional text directly reports learning-rate tolerance and ImageNet training-error comparisons. Conditioning measurements alone do not establish faster training.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors propose layer-wise conditioning analysis, report that BN stabilizes training and improves conditioning while sometimes permitting harmful weight domination, and attribute an important optimization difficulty in very deep ResNets to the last linear layer. Adding BN before that layer improves training. Their diagnosis is an experimental interpretation, not proof that this layer explains every source of residual-network optimization difficulty.
record.recipe_differences: Layer-wise conditioning analysis and training-loss experiments; the paper does not reproduce the claim versions’ principal training-error or stability-bound measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Training behavior varies with initialization (random versus He), normalization (Plain versus BN), network depth, and adding BN before the final linear layer.

fits_no_version.finding: BN improves layer-wise conditioning, preserves activation and gradient magnitudes, and reduces dying/full neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: BN improves these optimization diagnostics; the diagnostics alone do not establish faster accuracy gains or higher learning-rate tolerance.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix C.2 observes initial gradient explosion followed by weight domination in a 100-layer BN MLP and a 110-layer BN VGG-style network.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: BN does not universally prevent pathological gradient dynamics in very deep plain networks; these measurements do not establish the comparative training-speed effect named in V6.

fits_no_version.finding: The 2402-layer ResNetLastBN achieves test error of 5.04 ± 0.30.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The modified network achieves this generalization performance; test error alone does not measure the versions' training outcomes.

record.code_released: https://github.com/facebook/fb.resnet.torch (Torch implementation used for the ResNet setup; no study-code release is stated)
record.problems: The principal conditioning results are often figure-based; many training-loss values are not tabulated. The paper reports selected best losses across listed learning rates for some experiments. It does not provide training classification-error comparisons matching most versions.
record.rows_left_out: Deliberately blocked-weight-update experiments in Figure 4 and Appendix Figure A12 measure the effect of simulated weight domination, not ordinary BN or initialization training. Test-error tables on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 and ImageNet are not training-error outcomes. Other curvature spectra and neuron-count measurements do not directly measure a version’s named training outcome.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, and the specified size, early-stopping and regularization comparisons.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious-local-minimum frequencies and benefits of one or two extra student neurons.
Matched plain-versus-residual training-error comparisons, persistent plain-network degradation after longer training, very deep plain tanh networks, and Fixup.
A readable quantitative training-speed comparison, a sweep establishing maximum trainable depth, orthogonal-versus-Gaussian tanh initialization, and 10,000-layer plain convolutional networks.
Learning rates referenced to the initial linearized stability limit, squared-loss catapult dynamics, sharpness tracking the stability threshold and divergence despite starting below it.
The original sigmoid-MNIST and Inception-ImageNet settings, quantitative accuracy-gain rates for the conditioning experiments, and comparisons with Fixup.

missing.what: Separate learning-rate-tolerance outcomes: unnormalized 20-layer VGG-style and residual networks fail to converge at 0.1; additional runs at 0.01 are reported. Record BN and unnormalized recipes separately.
missing.locator: Appendix C.1, CNN for CIFAR-10 Classification, Figures A8-A9

missing.what: Top-1 training-error trajectories for ImageNet ResNet versus ResNetLastBN at depths 18 and 50. The authors explicitly report better optimization efficiency at both depths; these training errors are omitted despite the record's blanket characterization of appendix results as test outcomes.

Depth comparison within ResNetLastBN: nearly equal loss across depths during the first 80 epochs, followed by lower loss with increasing depth. This directly records how the additional normalization changes depth-dependent optimization.

The 1202-layer pre-activation ablation: removing its final extra BN produces a stalled weight-domination phase; retaining that BN avoids the problem. Record the training-loss trajectories separately from conditioning diagnostics.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for any listed version. Loss-based optimization evidence is distinguished from classification error, conditioning diagnostics and test performance. Figure-only numerical trajectories cannot be reconstructed reliably from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, and effects of model size, early stopping, or regularization.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student spurious minima and effects of student width.

The paper does not compare plain networks with and without identity shortcuts, or report the stated ImageNet/CIFAR-10 training-error comparison at matched depth. It tests depth-related training behavior in residual networks and a last-layer BN change.
The paper compares random and He initialization in MLPs but does not test the listed initialization methods, orthogonal weights, or 10,000-layer plain CNNs.
Learning rates above stability limits, curvature-threshold behavior, and divergence boundaries.

The paper reports BN-related training-loss behavior and conditioning, but does not report the specified accuracy-gain rates or learning-rate tolerance comparison across sigmoid MNIST, VGG CIFAR-10, and Inception ImageNet.

rows.subject: ResNetLastBN
rows.operation_detail: Added one BN layer before the last linear layer and trained on CIFAR-10.
rows.note: The authors report this result after describing doubled training iterations and weight decay 0.0002.
rows.check: The reported 5.04 ± 0.30 is test error, which cannot establish training-error degradation or training speed. Separate the successful-training comparison from this generalization outcome.

rows.subject: Plain MLP
rows.operation_detail: Trained with random initialization; layer-input and output-gradient magnitudes and training loss monitored.
rows.measure: Layer input/output-gradient magnitude and training loss
rows.note: Text reports exponential decrease in layer input and output-gradient magnitude; the selected training loss is the best among learning rates {0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1}.
rows.check: The conventional initialization produces vanishing signals and gradients, the predicted adverse side of the initialization comparison; this is not partial evidence merely because the initialization performs poorly. Separate these diagnostics from the unreadable training-loss curve.

rows.subject: Plain MLP
rows.operation_detail: Trained with He initialization; layer-input and output-gradient magnitudes and training loss monitored.
rows.measure: Layer input/output-gradient magnitude and training loss
rows.note: Text says He initialization makes layer input/output-gradient magnitude stable across layers; no exact training-loss value is stated.
rows.check: He initialization preserves signal and gradient magnitudes and is explicitly described as relieving the diagnosed problem. No exact loss, convergence-time advantage or depth limit can be recovered from the supplied figure transcription.

rows.subject: BN MLP
rows.operation_detail: Trained with batch normalization; layer-input and output-gradient magnitudes and training loss monitored.
rows.measure: Layer input/output-gradient magnitude and training loss
rows.note: Text says BN preserves input/output-gradient magnitude across layers for both initialization methods and relieves instability.
rows.check: The text establishes preserved magnitudes and stabilization, but does not explicitly quantify faster loss reduction, accuracy gain or learning-rate tolerance for this comparison. Split the diagnostics from training loss; the supplied figure transcription does not resolve the loss curves.

rows.check: Similar conditioning and stabilization observations under SGD do not by themselves establish faster training. The training-loss curve lacks a readable comparative value or trajectory in the supplied transcription.
